Hacker News #5

AI is killing All About Berlin

AI is killing All About Berlin

AI 作者 grey-area 热度 805 回复 710 2026/11/18 14:47
打开原帖 打开外部链接 JSON

摘要

  • Posted on May 26, 2026 Psst! There is an update to this post.
  • This is the traffic to All About Berlin, the website that I run since 2017, and live from since 2020. After 7 years of growth, it has lost 70% 75% of its traffic to Google AI Overviews. When you Googled something, you used to get a link to my website. Now you get a page of ads, then an AI-generated answer trained on my content, then finally a link to my website. This has a devastating impact on traffic. What it means to be first on Google It’s hard to fund my work with only a quarter of my audience. Soon, I will need another way to pay my rent. Instead of writing new guides, I already spend my days preparing for that future. It’s not just about the money. I have poured 8 years of my life into making something good and useful. Strangers’ faces light up when they learn that I run All About Berlin. Local and federal government offices refer people to my guides. The Berlin immigration office uses my data about themselves. It inspired two government portals and a few similar websites in other cities. If my work just get mixed into an AI-generated answer, I lose my voice and my audience. My carefully chosen words lose their meaning. No one shakes my hand and buys me a beer. No one tells me how their citizenship application went. This is not an isolated case. Many website owners have reached out in private to commiserate. Some have paywalled their work. Others have given up and moved on. They keep the websites online, but they no longer update them. It’s just not worth it. It will get worse. Last week, Google has made two announcements: AI-generated answers will replace search results entirely, and they have ads in them.1 This is the future of the internet. No websites, just a chat box with ads. I don’t know where All About Berlin fits in that future.

asdff 2026/11/19 03:04
Rideshare is interesting because uber et al might actually be cheaper per ride than waymo et al. Yes, they pay a driver a very low wage which is some overhead, but they don't own any cars. The driver pays for the car, its maintenance, registration and insurance, fueling, and storage. It is dubious if it even pencils out for anyone but the power users in the gig economy. Waymo has massive overhead with its fleet requirements, on the other hand, real estate requirements as well.

AI could be similar. The costs of the bleeding edge are probably enormous. But imagine if your competitor was some cheap model, with a layer of southeast asians between the user and the model getting the apparent quality of the model far higher leveraging some cheap expert human prompters. There's some odds there that they might route you at the bleeding edge. Plus also, plenty of users probably aren't even that sensitive to a low quality vs high quality response for their purposes.

majormajor 2026/11/18 16:56
AI and old-money protectionism are likely going exactly the same place: access to more things for old-money, reduced opportunities to carve out new things for those without. Just copy the new faster and cheaper than ever. Embrace-extend-extinguish at a class-level.

So many of the things that can be automated away don't really have higher-level value chains to move to. The value was other people reducing friction for you or presenting you with novelty. The AI-maximalist/old-money goals here are identical: avoid having to pay a person for that.

The core underlying assumption in both POVs—whether "shape rotators" or "old money elites"—is that everything boils down to manipulating abstractions. The world, to these groups, isn't about people living satisfying individual lives. It's about making things as convenient for themselves as possible, not about doing concrete things in the real world for people as a whole. They are (intentionally) replacing the territory with the map.
